rationale: Both sayings reject dishonest weights and scales before the Lord: the source calls deceitful scales an abomination, while the target calls a double weight an abomination and deceitful scales not good.
Insolence brings dishonor in the source, while the target places an exalted heart before ruin and humility before glory.
The righteous person's death leaves regret in the source; the target preserves the righteous person's memory with praise, contrasting the impious person's extinguished name.
Righteousness cuts blameless paths straight in the source; acknowledging wisdom likewise straightens one's ways and prevents stumbling in the target.
Both passages explicitly make righteousness a means of rescue, while denying lasting benefit to lawlessness.
The source says the righteous person's hope does not perish at death; the target explains that those apparently dead remain at peace with hope full of immortality.
The impious person is handed over in the escaping righteous person's place; the target similarly makes the lawless person a cleansing-offering for the righteous.
Both oppose the destructive or deceitful speech of the impious to the saving or successful discernment and speech of the upright.
The source attributes a city's prosperity to the good things of the righteous; the target similarly attributes a nation's exaltation to righteousness.
Impious mouths raze a city in the source; pestilent men set a city ablaze in the target, which adds the counteraction of wise people turning away wrath.
The intelligent person keeps quiet instead of sneering at citizens; the target likewise associates making oneself mute with appearing intelligent.
The source contrasts revealing council plans with faithfully concealing matters; Sirach explains that revealing secrets destroys trust and a close friendship.
Both use steering language and associate deliberation or much counsel with help and deliverance.
The source warns that an evil person harms a righteous associate; the target specifies that a lawless friend leads companions into bad ways.
The source's first contrast concerns a woman's contribution to her husband's glory or dishonor; the target calls a courageous woman his crown and an evil woman his destruction.
The merciful person benefits his own life in the source; Jesus similarly promises that the merciful will themselves receive mercy.
The source connects righteous seed with a true reward, while Galatians develops the principle that what one sows determines what one reaps and urges persistence in doing good.
Both contrast the life associated with righteousness against a morally destructive way leading to death.
Both explicitly say that the blameless are acceptable to the Lord; the source contrasts their ways with perverted ways that He abhors.
Both warn that one who unjustly puts hands into a hand will not escape punishment or receive acquittal; the source also contrasts righteous sowing and its reward.
The source's pig-ring image exposes beauty joined to bad judgment; the target likewise calls beauty vain and instead blesses an understanding woman.
Both explicitly say that the hope of the impious perishes, contrasting it with the good desire or enduring gladness of the righteous.
The source describes those who sow their own possessions and gain more; Paul likewise connects generous sowing with abundant reaping and God's multiplication of seed for righteousness.
The source blesses the person who shares grain rather than withholding it; the target promises nourishment to the person who gives his own loaves to the poor.
Evil overtakes the person who seeks it in the source; the target describes evils pursuing sinners and good things overtaking the righteous.
Both reject confidence in wealth; the target explicitly redirects the rich toward God, good works, and generous sharing, corresponding to the source's positive support of righteous people.
The source's second clause makes the fool serve an intelligent person; the target likewise elevates an intelligent household servant over foolish masters.
Righteousness bears a tree of life in the source; wisdom, whose mouth produces righteousness in the target's context, is herself a tree of life to those holding her fast.
First Peter quotes the source's question about the righteous being saved with difficulty and where the impious and sinner will appear, applying it within a discussion of judgment and suffering.
Both commend receiving rebukes and expose rejection of discipline as destructive: the source calls it foolish, while the target calls it hatred of oneself.
The source commends finding favor with the Lord over lawlessness; the target identifies devout hearts and blameless people as those He loves and accepts.
The source's righteous roots cannot be uprooted; the target expresses the same enduring stability by saying that the righteous will never give way.
A courageous wife crowns her husband in the source; finding a good wife brings favors and gladness from God in the target.
The source contrasts righteous reasonings with deceptive steering; the target similarly contrasts devising evil with devising mercy and truth.
The source connects impious or upright speech with deceit or rescue; Jesus likewise connects speech with the speaker's moral character and with condemnation or justification.
Both contrast the disappearance of the impious or their houses with the continued standing of righteous households.
The source links an understanding mouth with praise; the target shows that even a senseless person can be reckoned intelligent through asking for wisdom and keeping silent.
The source contrasts self-support despite dishonor with an honored appearance that lacks bread; the target likewise distinguishes a rich appearance without possessions from humility amid wealth.

The righteous person's compassion for animals is given concrete expression in the law requiring restoration of a straying animal and help for an animal collapsed under its load, even when owned by an enemy.
Both say that working one's own land fills a person with bread; the source says those pursuing empty things lack understanding, while the target says those pursuing leisure are filled with poverty.
The source links lingering over wine with dishonor at home; the target identifies wine and drunkenness with indiscipline, insolence, and loss of wisdom.
Both identify the desires of the impious as evil; the target contrasts them with the righteous person's unsparing mercy and compassion.
Sinful lips trap the sinner in the source; the target likewise calls the fool's lips a trap for his life and his mouth his ruin.

The source opposes gentle treatment receiving mercy to confrontational behavior crushing lives; the target likewise contrasts a yielding answer that turns away wrath with painful speech that arouses it.
Both say that a person is filled from the fruit of his mouth and lips, making speech consequential for the speaker's own life.
Fools regard their own ways as upright in the source; the target broadens the warning that every person appears righteous to himself while the Lord sets hearts straight.
Both contrast a fool's exposed anger with prudent restraint: the source's resourceful person conceals dishonor, while the target's wise person stores up anger portion by portion.
Both contrast faithful, truthful witness with the deceitful testimony of an unjust witness.
The source contrasts speech that wounds like a sword with wise tongues that heal; the target similarly describes good words as sweet and healing to life.
The source contrasts truthful testimony with an unjust tongue; the law forbids accepting an empty report or joining an unrighteous witness to distort judgment.
The source promises joy to those who desire peace rather than devise evil; Jesus likewise blesses people who make peace.
Nothing unjust pleases the righteous in the source; the target positively identifies doing judgment as the righteous person's joy.
The source calls lying lips an abomination to the Lord; the law concretely forbids an empty report and agreement with an unrighteous witness.
The source locates discernment in an understanding person rather than a fool's heart; the target similarly locates wisdom in a good heart and denies it in fools' hearts.
The source contrasts a frightening word that troubles the heart with gladness from good news; the target likewise says that a good report replenishes the bones and good sights gladden the heart.
The source explicitly says that evils pursue sinners; the target repeats this statement and contrasts good things overtaking the righteous.
Both identify life with walking in righteousness; the target joins righteousness with mercy, complementing the source's warning against remembering wrongs.

The source commends a son's obedience to his father and warns of destruction through disobedience; Ephesians commands children to obey and honor parents and cites the promise of well-being and long life.
Both connect the fruit of righteousness with life and explicitly warn that lawless lives perish before their time.
Both say that guarding one's mouth preserves one's life, with the target expressly adding protection from affliction.
Both portray the idle person as occupied by desire while failing to act with his hands; the target states that such desires kill him.
The righteous person hates an unjust word in the source; the target likewise says that the righteous pays no attention to lying lips, unlike the evil listener.
Righteousness guards the innocent in the source; the target makes the protection concrete as rescue from death, in contrast to useless lawless treasures.
The contrast between a rich appearance with nothing and humility amid wealth parallels the target's contrast between outward honor without bread and a dishonored person who supports himself.

The source's first clause identifies wealth as a ransom for life; the target supplies a concrete instance in which a caught thief gives all his possessions and rescues himself. It does not repeat the source's separate claim about poverty and threats.
The source says the light of the impious is extinguished; the target applies the same image of an extinguished lamp and darkness to someone speaking evil of parents.
Both set the compassion and mercy of the righteous against the sinful or evil pursuits of the impious.
Both contrast insolence with wisdom; the source associates insolence with evil actions, while the target identifies its dishonor and locates wisdom with humility.
The source says lawlessly pursued property diminishes and commends compassionate lending; the target describes interest-based accumulation eventually going to someone merciful to the poor.
The source prefers beginning to help the heart over merely promising and raising hope; James gives the concrete case of comforting words to a needy person without supplying the necessities.
Both contrast respect for a command with destructive disregard: the target explicitly says that keeping a command guards life while despising one's ways leads to perishing.
The source promises success to a wise household servant in contrast to a deceitful son; the target likewise places an intelligent servant above foolish masters within the household.
Both describe authoritative wisdom or the Lord's command as a fountain of life opposed to a trap of death.
Both expressly say that knowing the law belongs to a good mind; the source embeds this in a contrast with contemptuous ways ending in destruction.
The resourceful person acts with knowledge in the source; the target specifies recognition of one's own ways as resourceful wisdom, in contrast to foolish wandering.
A faithful messenger rescues a king in the source; the target likewise describes the life-giving benefit a faithful messenger brings to those who sent him.
The source ties accepting discipline and rebukes to improvement and honor; the target urges listening to a father's discipline so as to become wise later in life.
The source calls devout desires sweet to life; the target similarly calls every desire of the righteous good, contrasting impious hopes that perish.
The source says that walking with the wise makes one wise; Sirach supplies the practice of clinging to wise elders, listening, and repeatedly visiting an understanding person.
Both explicitly say that evils pursue those who sin; the source adds the contrary prospect of good things overtaking the righteous.
The source says the impious person's wealth is stored for the righteous; Ecclesiastes likewise describes the sinner gathering possessions to hand them to the person good before God.
The source contrasts the righteous person's many years with the unjust person's swift death; the target similarly contrasts added days through fear of the Lord with shortened impious years.
The source treats careful discipline as an expression of a father's love; Hebrews makes that association explicit for God's discipline while also discussing earthly fathers and its intended benefit.
The source contrasts the righteous person's satisfying food with impious want; the target expressly says that the Lord will not starve a righteous life.
Wise women build houses in the source; the target likewise makes wisdom and understanding the means of building and establishing a house and filling its stores.
The source connects upright walking with fear of the Lord; the target similarly commands fear of God together with turning away from evil.
The wise person's lips guard him in the source; the target likewise makes guarding one's mouth a way of keeping one's life, in contrast with rash speech.
The source explicitly recognizes the ox's strength behind abundant produce; the law's prohibition on muzzling a threshing ox likewise recognizes the working animal's contribution to grain production.
The source opposes a faithful witness who does not lie to an unjust witness who kindles lies; the law prohibits agreement with an unrighteous witness and acceptance of an empty report.
Both deny that wisdom can be found with evil or impious people; the source contrasts the ready discernment found among the intelligent.
The source makes recognizing one's own ways the wisdom of the resourceful; the target similarly says that the upright person understands his ways.
The source contrasts disappearing impious houses with standing righteous tents; the target likewise gives strength to righteous houses while impious roots and fruits perish.
Both warn that ways appearing upright to a person nevertheless end at the bottom of Hades.
The source says that a rash or good person is filled from his own ways or thoughts; Galatians expresses the same consequential relation as reaping what one has sown, whether corruption or life.
The source warns against believing every word and commends reconsideration; John applies that caution to spiritual claims, requiring testing rather than believing every spirit.
Both connect fear with turning from evil and oppose it to confidence in one's own judgment or wisdom.
The source links quick anger with acting without counsel; James commands slowness to anger and explains that human anger does not accomplish God's righteousness.

The source contrasts fools inheriting wickedness with resourceful people gaining discernment; the target illustrates the difference through a resourceful person learning from punishment while fools pass by and suffer it.
Both contrast the rich person's many friends with the abandonment or hostility experienced by a poor friend.
The source blesses mercy toward the poor instead of dishonoring them; the target describes that mercy as a loan to God which He will repay.
The source identifies mercy and truth with good plans and actions; the target identifies the same qualities as the guard of a king and support of his righteous throne.
The source contrasts abundance from taking care with want from pleasure-seeking; the target makes the contrast concrete as cultivating one's land versus pursuing empty things.
Both contrast faithful testimony with the deceit of an unjust witness; the source additionally identifies faithful witness as rescuing life.
The source associates fear of the Lord with strength and support left to children; the target likewise says that blameless righteous living leaves one's children blessed.
The Lord's command is a fountain of life that turns one from death's trap; the target assigns the same life-giving fountain image to the wise person's law.
Both explicitly associate patience with understanding or intelligence; the source contrasts it with the folly of being faint of spirit, while the target also commends restraint of harsh speech.
Both say that mistreating a poor person provokes the One who made him; both also contrast such conduct with compassion and mercy.

Both describe the impious person being removed or disappearing; the source identifies trust in one's piety with righteousness, while the target adds an explicit promise of lasting preservation for the righteous.
Wisdom resides in a good heart in the source; the target positively describes the intelligent heart acquiring discernment and wise ears seeking reflection.
The source says righteousness exalts a nation; the target concretely assigns the raising of a country to a righteous king and its destruction to a lawless man.
The source commends an intelligent attendant accepted by a king; the target likewise places a perceptive, skillful worker beside kings rather than sluggish men.
The source's yielding answer turns away wrath; the target likewise attributes effective power to patience and a soft tongue.
Both associate wise or righteous speech with knowledge, contrasting the speech or fate of fools.
The source says the Lord's eyes are everywhere observing good and evil; the target likewise describes His eyes looking through the whole earth, here to strengthen hearts whole toward Him.
Both expressly describe the tongue's ability to heal, with the source representing that healing as a tree of life.

The source contrasts a fool's contempt for paternal discipline with resourceful command-keeping; the target likewise contrasts an understanding, law-keeping son with one whose dissipation dishonors his father.

The source gives strength to righteous households while the impious perish root and fruit; the target similarly contrasts the impious person's disappearance with the righteous person's enduring salvation.
The source binds wise lips to discernment; the target likewise depicts the wise heart carrying discernment upon the lips.
Both call the sacrifices of the impious an abomination to the Lord; the target makes explicit that these offerings are made lawlessly.
Both contrast the Lord's abhorrence of evil ways with His acceptance or love of those whose ways are righteous and blameless.
The source warns that hatred of rebukes ends in shameful death; the target likewise opposes life-preserving obedience to destructive contempt for one's ways.
Both explicitly say that Hades and destruction are exposed before God; Proverbs uses this as the basis for its further claim about human hearts.
The source's uneducated person avoids reprovers and wise companions; Sirach commands the contrary practice of staying with wise elders, listening, and seeking out understanding people.
Both contrast bodily flourishing from a rejoicing heart with the bodily harm or gloom associated with sorrow.
The upright heart seeks discernment in the source; the target similarly describes the intelligent heart acquiring discernment and wise ears seeking reflection.
The source contrasts evil people's constant expectation of evils with good people's quiet rest; the target promises the listener to Wisdom rest without fear of every evil.
Both prefer a smaller or poorer material condition with godly conduct to wealth compromised by moral failure: fear of the Lord versus fearlessness here, truth versus lying there.
Both prefer a modest meal enjoyed in friendship or peace to abundant food or possessions accompanied by enmity and battle.
The source contrasts a quick-tempered maker of battles with a patient peacemaker; James urges slowness to anger because human anger does not accomplish God's righteousness.

relationship: parallel escalation and calming of strife
rationale: The source contrasts patience that extinguishes disputes with impiety that inflames them; the target similarly contrasts hatred that raises strife with friendship that covers those averse to it.
Both say that a wise son makes his father glad and contrast a foolish son's harmful relation to his mother.
The intelligent person makes his course straight in the source; the target similarly connects acknowledging wisdom with straightened ways and freedom from stumbling.
The source credits lasting counsel to those who deliberate; the target likewise locates help in a deliberative heart, specifically in conducting war.
The source describes understanding as ways of life that avert Hades; the target likewise locates life in righteous ways and death in the ways of those remembering wrongs.
The Lord establishes the widow's boundary in the source; the target prohibits moving boundaries or invading orphans' property because the Lord will defend their case.
The source condemns unjust thought and commends pure sayings; the target similarly distinguishes righteous reasonings from the deceptive designs of the impious.

relationship: legal counterpart for refusal of bribes
rationale: The source commends hating gifts that bring self-destruction; the law forbids gifts that justify the ungodly, blind the eyes, and corrupt righteous words.
The source says acts of mercy and faithfulness cleanse sins; Sirach likewise compares almsgiving's atonement for sins to water extinguishing fire.

relationship: parallel fear and avoidance of evil
rationale: The source's second clause says fear of the Lord turns everyone from evil; the target directly commands fear of God and turning away from every evil.
The source contrasts righteous meditation on faithful things with evil answers from the impious; Jesus similarly traces good or evil speech to the moral contents of the heart.
The source links God-pleasing righteous ways with enemies becoming friends; Romans instructs peaceful conduct and practical kindness toward enemies as a way of overcoming evil with good.
Both contrast God's attention to righteous prayers with His opposition or distance toward evildoers.
The source prefers a small righteous gain to abundant unjust produce; the target similarly prefers a truthful poor person to a lying rich person.
The source urges righteous consideration so that God may set a person's steps right; the target likewise attributes the directing of human steps to the Lord.
The source links a glad heart and good report with replenished bones; the target similarly contrasts bodily flourishing from a rejoicing heart with dried bones under sorrow.
The source calls keeping rebukes love of one's own life; the target likewise identifies acquiring understanding as loving oneself.
Both explicitly connect fear of God or the Lord with wisdom and its beginning or discipline.

Both say that an evil day awaits the impious: the source specifies that he will perish on it, while the target says he is kept for it. Their first clauses concern different subjects, humble people's works and the Lord's works.
The source calls the high-hearted person unclean before God; James likewise says God opposes the proud and calls for humility before Him.
Both explicitly prefer doing righteous things before God to offering sacrifices; the target adds speaking truth to this ethical priority.
The source promises knowledge with righteousness to those seeking the Lord rightly; James similarly directs anyone lacking wisdom to ask God in faith and expect His generous gift.
The source declares all the Lord's works righteous; the target likewise calls His works pure and upright while distinguishing the crooked ways allotted to crooked people.
The source describes a king's mouth as reliable in judgment; Solomon's judgment about the child leads Israel to recognize God's discernment within him for carrying out justice.
Both connect just weights with the Lord's approval or righteousness; the target contrasts them with deceitful scales that He abhors.
The source says a throne of rule is prepared through righteousness; the target similarly surrounds the king's throne with righteousness, mercy, and truth.
The source's king loves upright speech; the psalmic speaker similarly receives the faithful and blameless into service while refusing success to those speaking unjust things before him.
The source calls a king's wrath a messenger of death; the target compares a king's threat to a lion's growling, emphasizing the danger of royal displeasure.

relationship: shared royal favor and moisture imagery
rationale: The source compares acceptance by the king's son to a cloud of late rain; the target likewise compares royal cheerfulness to dew on grass.
Both value wisdom and understanding above gold and silver; the target extends the comparison to costly stones and all precious things.
The source links receiving discipline and guarding one's ways with preserving life; the target likewise makes keeping a command a guard for life and warns against despising one's ways.
Both explicitly place an exalted or insolent disposition before ruin; the target adds humility before glory as the counterpattern.
The source prefers gentleness and humility to sharing spoils with the insolent; James grounds the same preference in God's opposition to the proud and grace toward the humble.
The source pronounces the person trusting God blessed; the target commands wholehearted trust in God rather than self-exaltation in one's own wisdom.
Reflection is a fountain of life in the source; the target applies the same image to the wise person's law, contrasting it with senseless death.
The source joins a wise heart with discerning lips; Jesus likewise describes speech as emerging from the heart's store and distinguishes good from evil speakers.
Good words heal life in the source; the target similarly makes the healing of a tongue a tree of life.
Both warn that ways which appear upright to a person nevertheless end at the bottom of Hades.
The source's concluding clause places destruction on the crooked person's own mouth; the target likewise calls a fool's mouth his ruin and his lips a trap for his life.
The source depicts an evildoer storing fire on his lips; James expands the tongue-as-fire image to its power to ignite and stain an entire life.
The source says crooked, deceitful conduct separates friends; the target identifies exposing rather than concealing wrongdoings as a further way to separate friends and household members.
The source warns that a lawless friend leads others into bad ways; the target commands avoiding an angry companion lest one learn his ways and acquire life-threatening snares.

relationship: parallel eyes used for harmful intent
rationale: The source joins fixed eyes, perverted thought, and evil speech; the target likewise describes deceitful eye-signaling that brings grief to others.
The source calls old age a crown of boasting found in righteousness; the target similarly calls gray hair the glory of elders.

relationship: parallel moral capacity over physical strength
rationale: The source ranks patience and control of anger above strength and capturing a city; the target similarly ranks a wise person above a strong one.
